edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1      1 (page number set apart at the right, on every page)
edits.fix: Use the standard footer "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>" in the page template.

edits.quote: Find all the ways to cover each shape with blue blocks. Put each way on a shape of its own. (3 outlines of the small hexagon, which has only 2 coverings; 4 outlines of the long hexagon, which has only 3)
edits.fix: K-1 children will try to fill every outline and end up repeating a covering or deciding they failed. Print 2 small hexagons and 3 long hexagons so that filling the outlines means finding all the ways.

edits.quote: Draw each way on a small shape. (8 half-size outlines, triangle edge 0.5 in, for a 16-triangle hexagon that has 6 coverings)
edits.fix: Kindergartners cannot reliably draw 8-rhombus coverings on half-inch triangles. Replace these with 6 actual-size outlines (two per page) so children can build each covering with blocks and leave it in place, as in P3, and change the sentence to "Put each way on a shape of its own."

k-1.summary: A strong K-1 set. It has six real problems on actual-size boards: telling possible from impossible shapes (including two even-area shapes that still cannot be covered), fewest green blocks, counting coverings, fewest blocks with mixed pieces, and a placement game whose answers (first, second, first, first, second) are all correct. The only real problems are with recording: extra outlines in P3 imply coverings that do not exist, and in P6 children must draw coverings on half-size shapes, which is too fine for five-year-olds.

edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1      1 (page number set apart at the right, on every page)
edits.fix: Use the standard footer "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>" in the page template.

edits.quote: Then explain why nobody can cover the biggest triangle with fewer green triangles than you used. (The side-5 triangle and the writing lines sit on page 4, which has no problem label. On page 3 the biggest triangle a child can see is the side-4 one.)
edits.fix: Say "the biggest triangle (on the next page)", or mark page 4 as the continuation of Problem 3, so children explain the side-5 case and do not stop after page 3.

edits.quote: If you cover it with blue rhombuses and green triangles, what is the fewest number of green triangles you need? What if the board has 100 small triangles along each side?
edits.fix: As written, a child can answer by continuing the pattern 2, 3, 4, 5 without any reasoning. Add "Explain how you know, without drawing the board," so that the child has to count up and down triangles row by row (55 up, 45 down) and say where the greens go.

edits.quote: Find a rule that tells which places for the two green triangles work, and explain why your rule is right.
edits.fix: The rule is that one green points up and one points down (all 144 such placements work). Proving that every such placement works is beyond grades 2-3. Change the request to "explain why places that break your rule can never work" and leave the converse to the adult.

grades-2-3.summary: This is the strongest band. It develops the up/down coloring obstruction through a well-chosen sequence: possible and impossible boards (including the even-area trapezoid and the bow-tie that is balanced but cannot be covered), boards with holes, fewest greens for sides 2 to 5, the general case, chevrons that can never do better, designing a board that needs 6 greens, and a rule for placing two holes. I checked every board and every answer, and all are correct. The only edits are a page break with no label and two prompts that should ask for reasoning matched to the age group.

edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1      1 (page number set apart at the right, on every page)
edits.fix: Use the standard footer "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>" in the page template.

edits.quote: On the small boards below, draw all your coverings from Problem 1 again.
edits.fix: Copying six coverings a second time is busywork. Have children letter their coverings in Problem 1 and draw the flip graph below using the letters, and remove the 8 repeat boards.

edits.quote: Start with any covering of the hexagon board from Problem 3. ... Find a way to do this with 4 flips that never flips the same hexagon twice in a row.
edits.fix: This cannot be done from covering E or F, which each have only one place to flip, and the board is left at F at the end of Problem 3. Write "Start with covering A" (A has three places to flip, and a 4-flip round trip exists).

edits.quote: Find a way to do this with 4 flips ... (only two blank lines for recording)
edits.fix: Add a small drawing of covering A on which children number the hexagons they flip 1 to 4, so they have a way to record the round trip.

edits.quote: On the hexagon board each covering has two ribbons, because its top side has two short edges.
edits.fix: The board in Problem 1 is also a hexagon. Write "On the board from Problem 3".

edits.quote: Draw them on the small hexagons below (25 hexagons with triangle edges about 0.3 in, for 20 coverings of 12 rhombi each)
edits.fix: The drawings are too small to show 12 rhombi legibly. Let children record each covering by its two ribbons (from Problem 5), and keep only a few larger hexagons for sketching.

grades-4-5.summary: This band covers kernel 2 faithfully and accurately: counting the six coverings of the 1-2-2 hexagon, the flip graph (diameter 4), flip distances A-B = 3, C-D = 4, E-F = 8 (all verified), parity of round trips, ribbons (the LRRLR example is drawn correctly), and the closing count of 20 for the 1-3-3 hexagon. The edits are small: P4 says "any covering", which fails for the two extreme coverings; P4 has no recording space for the flips; P2 has children redraw all their coverings; and the P7 drawing hexagons are too small.

overall.strongest: The grades 2-3 pages build the coloring obstruction through a contrasting, mathematically correct sequence of actual-size boards, ending with problems that ask children to invent a board and to find a rule.
overall.weakest: All the edits are small: the 4-5 P4 instruction to start from "any covering" fails for coverings E and F, and K-1 P6 asks very young children to draw coverings on half-size outlines.
